The chapter lists 17 consequences of leaving the thin-tailed comfort zone.  The
table below maps each one to a current or planned wiki atom.
The LLN may converge too slowly to be useful in finite samples.
The sample mean can badly miss the population or generating-process mean.
Variance and standard deviation can be unstable or undefined.
Beta, Sharpe ratio, and similar finance metrics inherit variance instability.
Planned Sharpe Ratio Under Heavy Tails
Robust or nonparametric summaries may hide the tail events that dominate payoff.
Planned Robust Statistics Under Heavy Tails
Least-squares regression loses its usual justification under thick-tailed errors.
Estimating a tail parameter and plugging it into a functional can outperform direct mean estimation.
Confirming a thin-tail story is harder than rejecting one after a large deviation.
PCA and factor models can manufacture unstable factors under heavy tails.
Moment matching fails when the target moments do not exist or are sample dominated.
Conditional on a large deviation, there may be no stable “typical” large deviation.
Concentration measures such as Gini can fail to aggregate additively.
Classical large-deviation tools are thin-tail tools and can fail for subexponential tails.
Planned Large Deviations vs. Heavy Tails
Dynamic hedging arguments depend on tail assumptions that fail in thick-tail regimes.
Forecasting event frequency is not the same as estimating expected payoff.
Rare-event psychology often confuses bounded calibration errors with unbounded payoff errors.
Ruin and path dependence require time-probability thinking, not only ensemble averages.
Planned Ruin Path Dependence and planned Ensemble vs. Time Probability

The forecasting section distinguishes probability estimates from exposures.
The LLN section then gives the practical reason this matters: for thick-tailed
variables, adding observations may not stabilize the sample mean at the speed
thin-tail habits expect.
Running-mean fan plot for Gaussian, Student-t, and Pareto samples.

Effective sample-size comparison for the same target error under Gaussian and
Pareto assumptions.
High-hit-rate strategy with rare ruin loss versus low-hit-rate convex payoff.

The chapter’s epistemology sections argue that absence of observed catastrophe
is weak evidence under thick tails.  The same logic explains why multiplicative
risks, contagion, and systemic losses should not be compared naively with
bounded or near-independent thin-tailed risks.
Planned Absence of Evidence Under Heavy Tails

These should be written with explicit caveats: the chapter’s examples are
decision and inference arguments, not proofs of any particular empirical model.

The final movement of the chapter shifts from estimating distributions to
surviving exposures.  The key wiki bridge is the distinction between ensemble
probability and time probability: an average across many parallel worlds is not
the same as the path followed by a single agent who can hit an absorbing ruin
barrier.
